Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

issues.explanation: The trigger items are not clinically coherent with the indexed trauma of a life-threatening motor vehicle collision. These cues imply military/combat and sexual-threat or specific geopolitical associations that are not plausibly linked to the reported trauma, and no accompanying threat, appraisal, or strategy items provide a bridge that would make these triggers understandable for this patient. By contrast, the memory items are internally coherent and fit severe reliving after an MVC, as well as the active Memory → Triggers formulation.

'Cars hit by accident' fits the trauma and aligns with the active Memory → Triggers formulation, but 'Sexual situations or intimacy' and 'Arab villages' imply very different trauma contexts (e.g., sexual trauma or combat/terrorism-related threat) that are not represented anywhere else in Memory, Threat, Appraisals, or Strategies. This makes the trigger profile hard to explain as belonging to the same patient and trauma.

For a 51-year-old male welder whose index trauma is a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, the trigger 'Arab villages' is hard to reconcile clinically with the stated trauma type and the rest of the profile. The memory items all concern vivid sensory/bodily reliving of a crash, which coheres with MVC trauma and the active Memory → Triggers edge, but 'Arab villages' implies a war-zone or ethnopolitical context that is not represented anywhere else in the self-report or formulation. This is a clearly implausible trigger for this trauma profile, unlike the crash imagery and alcohol smell triggers, which could plausibly cue MVC memories.

vignette: Tevita, a 51‑year‑old welder from the island of Viti Levu, spent most of his life in the glow of molten metal, the hiss of welding torches, and the steady rhythm of steel being joined. He and his wife, Aroha, had lived in a modest house for fifteen years, the sound of cars and trucks the soundtrack of their daily routine. One rainy evening in August, while driving home from a late shift, Tevita’s life turned on its head. A drunk driver, the seat of his car slipping into a lane that was closed for construction, slammed into the rear of Tevita’s vehicle. The impact was sudden and violent, the steering wheel buckling, metal cracking. He was thrown forward, his body pressed against the seat, his head striking the dashboard. The world exploded into noise: metal screeching, glass shattering, and a sudden, acrid smell of burning plastic. He emerged from the wreck, wounded, but alive. After the crash, the memory of that night did not fade. Instead, it settled into the deeper parts of his mind, a place where the scene could be replayed with alarming clarity. Whenever the sight of a car in a traffic jam, a news clip of a collision, or even a faint hum of an engine on the radio surfaced, Tevita’s body would snap back into the position he had held that night, his back and shoulders tense, his heart racing. The physical pain that had been lodged in his ribs during the crash returned in pulses, sharp and familiar, as if the injury had never healed. In those moments the memory was not simply a recollection; it was a full sensory reliving, complete with the smell of gasoline, the screeching of tires, and the metallic taste of blood on his tongue. When the memory surfaces, the triggers that had become inextricably linked to the event flare up automatically. The vividness of the scene pulls in the crash imagery: the sight of cars hitting each other, the flash of flashing lights, the blackened wreckage. The odor of alcohol, which Tevita had been exposed to at the bar that night before the crash, clings to the air, stirring a sense of danger and dread. The roar of engines and the clatter of clutches in traffic echo in his mind, making the world around him feel like an arena of imminent catastrophe. In one paragraph that a therapist could have written, it is clear that the memory of the collision gives rise to the triggers: “When the memory of the collision surfaces, the vivid body position and pain immediately ignite the crash imagery and car sounds that had become triggers, bringing the present environment into that terrifying moment.” The welding shop, once a sanctuary of focused labor, has become a minefield of stimuli that threaten to reopen the trauma. The hiss of the welding arc, the clanging of metal, and even the faint metallic tang of solder all echo the sounds Tevita had once heard on the highway. Whenever the shop’s lights flicker and the sound of an engine starts outside the workshop, he feels a jolt that forces him to retreat from the workbench. He has begun arriving late or skipping early shifts, telling his supervisor that he needs to check the truck’s oil or that the engine sounds are too loud. Aroha notices the change; she sees him pull back into the living room after the workday, avoiding the garage entirely. Tevita, for the first time since the crash, avoids the very environment that once defined his identity. Weeks turned into months, and the pattern of feeling the body in that same position, the pain returning, and the sensory flood that flooded the present grew more entrenched. The welding shop’s sounds became less tolerable, the traffic outside his window a constant reminder of the collision’s echoes. He began to dread the simple act of driving, the routine that had once been a safe commute. The weight of the unresolved memories and the intensity of the triggers had begun to sap his energy, leaving him exhausted even after a full day at work. It is this mounting anxiety and the fear of losing his livelihood that finally led Tevita to seek help. He worries that if he cannot return to the shop, he will lose his sense of purpose and his connection to his wife and family. He hopes to find a way to stay grounded in the present, to keep the memory from commandeering his life, and to reclaim the sound of his own heartbeat without the echo of a crash. He brings his story to the therapist with a trembling voice, asking, “I don’t want to live like this—stuck in a loop of pain and danger. I just want to put my hand on the welding torch again without my heart pounding like it’s the end of the world.”
